properties.description: The home on-site is built on a bluff, which is armored by a two-tiered approximately 200 LF concrete bulkhead and upland retaining wall. An engineer inspection revealed that the lower bulkheads are damaged and require repairs. The proposed project is to repair the bulkhead in two phases. Proposed activities for Phase 1 include the repair of the upper bulkhead by sealing cracks and recoating the metal piles with an anti-corrosive coating. Proposed activities for Phase 2 include patching and recoating of the concrete headwall, repairing the 12 concrete buttresses, and installing a steel sheet pile at the lower bulkhead footing for the entire length of the bulkhead.

properties.description:
This project was based on dealing with water runoff. We have an active landslide to our north and others nearby. We had a scare and hired engineers to design us a retaining wall, which came in at more than 450k. One of them told us our home could be red tagged. Long story short, we didn't do the 450k solider wall and decided to go with just replacing what was already in place but adding water control for rain water. We also added safety rails, and stairs to replace rotten stairs or unsafe stairs, or in the case of the concrete stairs (main) it was to replace the historic concrete path that came up to the house but was broken and uneven in places (unsafe). So thats about it. We worked on it for a long time, and now its safe for my small kids, now the water all comes into the system insted of coming down the hill onto my neighbors (such as Peter M) who had to spent 250K on a retaining wall because of a slide on HIS property a number of years ago, but before we moved here. So yes, drainage - all using gravity which all ends up in the same system. That system ends in a water vault. 

Lastly, we have spent a huge amount of money on replanting already - with native plants. We're not doing all it on our own, and have a steep stope professional who comes to help. We are removing invasive and toxic vegatation very slowly as we replace the root space with native plants. 

Lastly I will add that we didn't disturb the soils. We just worked with the topography and especially in the case of the concrete path, we just used the footprint that was already there. I have some of those photos.

properties.description:
Detailed Description of Proposed Bamboo Barrier

We have been battling and removing invasive bamboo from neighbor's yard at 6309 Evanston North for many years.  We are now planning on installing a bamboo barrier.  The following is a description:

1.  Barrier will be set-back as appropriate from the existing concrete retaining wall.
2.  Barrier will run approximately 6-feet West to East, ending within 6-inches of the property line between Schiller's 523 N 64th and Redfield's 519 N 64th.   Specifically, this is on the front of the downhill side of the existing retaining wall dividing the two properties. 
3.  Barrier will run approximately 6-feet South to North along this same property line.
4.  Barrier will have structure permitting further building  up this N-S retaining wall mentioned in #2 above, along the East side of the barrier. 
5.  Tools: Reciprocating saw corded, with 12" long blade; hand tools, pick axe, shovels, pry bars, etc.
6.  A swath 8-10 inches wide is cut to install the bamboo barrier.  The barrier will be installed 18-inches below the surface (Note 1) with 6-inches of the barrier visible above  ground for a total of  2-feet. It is understood that this is the normal installation.

Note (1): The reference, "surface" is at the same ground level as the Schiller's yard.  

7.  The bamboo barrier will be installed 18-inches below this surface. It will be placed on the Redfield's property.  All sides of the barrier will be dug out to the same level.  Both the North-South side and the East-West side will be dug out to the same level.  Specifically, the existing "berm" on the Redfield's property will be dug out to the same depth right up to the edge of concrete retaining wall that separates Redfield's property from Scott's property.
 8.  The bamboo barrier, in the shape of a, "J," measures 6-feet by 6-feet with a North-South side and an East-West side.
 9.  There already exists a dig on Redfield's side of the adjoining corner properties about 3-feet deep where they have begun bamboo root system removal.  This plan involves installing a bamboo barrier, back-filling all of the dirt we are removing with some added new topsoil. 
10. Further the plan is to improve the landscaping of the yard by planting vegetation, shrubs or a tree that will beautify the area and provide room for gardening.  We believe that the root systems of this vegetation, once installed, will provide further strengthening of the integrity of the landscaping in this area.

properties.description:
The proposed Pier 1 demolition and replacement activities include:

(1)Demolition of the existing Pier 1 timber and concrete structure.
(2)Installation of a commercial grade pier and an adjacent marina facility within the previous pier footprint. Activity is anticipated to include installation of a sheet pile wall within a portion of the aquatic habitat below the existing pier. Filling activities will occur behind the sheet pile wall to support installation of the new pier and marina facility.
(3)

Restoration of the existing shoreline revetment adjacent to the new pier and marina.
(4)Shoreline excavation to create area of gravel beach to compensate for unavoidable aquatic habitat impacts.






The existing pier consists of approximately 1,900 creosote piles and is significantly deteriorated with only a perimeter concrete apron that is in any measure of serviceable use. Replacement of the pier is needed to maintain the industrial/commercial marine use of the pier.

Based on soil and groundwater investigations, it is reported that upland soil, composed predominately of fill materials, is contaminated with metals and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).

Restoration of the existing shoreline revetment is needed to prevent further erosion of the shoreline, and will assist in containing contaminated upland soils onsite.

Fill activities proposed below a portion of the existing pier's footprint, will partially utilize upland contaminated soils and suspected contaminated sediment (to the extent practicable) that will be disturbed during the course of  pier demolition and replacement activities and shoreline restoration. A sheet pile wall is proposed waterward of the area of fill to provide containment of the upland soil and dewatered sediment and protect the new pier structure. The new retaining wall feature will be contiguous with adjacent proposed shoreline revetment.

properties.description:
Ash Grove Cement Company (property owner) is applying for an emergency exemption from Shoreline Substantial Development requirements for the repair of a bulk product retaining wall on their property along the Lower Duwamish Waterway (LDW).  A portion of the retaining wall failed on March 16, 2015 and is in imminent need of repair to resume regular operations on the site.  
Ash Grove contacted the City of Seattle (Seattle Public Utilities; Mark Benson) immediately following the wall failure to determine the necessary steps to rectify the issue.  As such, Ash Grove is submitting this emergency exemption application to replace the failed section of retaining wall with a temporary Ecology/Kelly Block wall until a permanent structure can be designed, permitted, and constructed.
